short: A country's public money manager: it sets key interest rates, issues currency, and acts as banker to banks and the government.
kid: Think of a big grown-up who looks after the whole town's piggy bank. They decide how many coins go around and help the smaller piggy banks when they run short.
detail: A central bank is the institution responsible for the money and monetary system of a country or currency area. Its core jobs are keeping prices stable, setting the policy interest rate, issuing banknotes, managing liquidity in the banking system, acting as lender of last resort to banks in trouble, and often regulating banks and managing foreign-exchange reserves. Most modern central banks, such as the Federal Reserve and the ECB, are legally independent in day-to-day policy, and in India a committee sets rates without government direction, so that decisions are not driven by election cycles. Their moves ripple into loan rates, bond yields, currencies and stock valuations, which is why markets track every statement. A common confusion: a central bank does not take deposits from or lend to ordinary people and companies; it deals with banks, the government and markets.
example: When the RBI raises its repo rate by 0.25 percentage point (25 basis points), banks usually pass it on: a home loan linked to the repo rate at, say, 8.50% would reset to 8.75% at its next reset date.

short: India's central bank, set up in 1935, which sets the repo rate, issues banknotes, regulates banks and manages the country's foreign-exchange reserves.
kid: The RBI is like the head teacher of all the piggy banks in India. It makes the paper notes and keeps an eye on the other money-keepers so everyone plays fair.
detail: The Reserve Bank of India began operating on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, and was nationalised in 1949; it is headquartered in Mumbai and often called Mint Street in the press. Under the flexible inflation-targeting framework adopted in 2016, its main monetary job is to keep CPI inflation near a target set by the government for five-year periods: 4% within a 2-6% band under the framework as of 2025. Rate decisions are made by the six-member Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by the Governor. Beyond policy, the RBI issues currency, regulates and supervises banks and NBFCs, manages government borrowing, runs payment systems and manages forex reserves and the rupee. A common mix-up: SEBI, not the RBI, regulates the stock market; the RBI's reach is money, banks and payments.
example: Say the RBI's MPC cuts the repo rate by 25 basis points. A borrower with a ₹40 lakh floating home loan linked to the repo rate sees the rate fall by 0.25 percentage point at the next reset, saving roughly ₹10,000 of interest in the first year (₹40,00,000 × 0.25%).

short: The central bank of the United States, which sets the federal funds rate and whose decisions move interest rates, currencies and markets worldwide.
kid: The Fed looks after the money for all of America. So many people around the world use American dollars that when the Fed makes a choice, everyone feels it, like a big wave in a pool.
detail: The Federal Reserve System, created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, is the US central bank. It consists of a seven-member Board of Governors in Washington, DC, housed in the Eccles Building, twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks, and the Federal Open Market Committee, which sets policy. Its dual mandate is maximum employment and stable prices, and it defines price stability as 2% inflation on the PCE price index. Its main tool is the target range for the federal funds rate, supported by the interest it pays on bank reserves, balance-sheet policy such as quantitative easing, and bank supervision. Because the dollar is the world's main reserve and funding currency, Fed moves shift global capital flows, including foreign portfolio money into Indian stocks and bonds, and the rupee. The Fed Chair is its public face but holds one vote among twelve on the FOMC.
example: In March 2020 the Fed cut its target range to 0-0.25% to fight the Covid shock; between March 2022 and July 2023 it raised it eleven times to 5.25-5.50%, a total increase of 525 basis points.

short: The central bank for the countries that use the euro; it sets interest rates for the whole euro area from Frankfurt.
kid: Lots of neighbouring countries share the same kind of coins, the euro. The ECB is the one helper who looks after those shared coins for all of them together.
detail: The European Central Bank, based in Frankfurt and operating since 1998, sets monetary policy for all euro-area countries. Together with their national central banks it forms the Eurosystem, which carries out operations such as lending to banks. Its primary mandate under the EU treaties is price stability, defined since its 2021 strategy review as 2% inflation over the medium term, with misses either side treated as equally bad. The Governing Council, made up of the six Executive Board members and the euro-area national central bank governors, sets three key rates: the deposit facility rate, which now steers money-market rates, the main refinancing operations rate and the marginal lending facility rate. Its unique challenge is that one interest rate must suit economies as different as Germany and Greece. Do not confuse it with the European Commission, or with the 27-country EU, not all of which uses the euro.
example: Say a euro-area bank keeps €100 million at the ECB's deposit facility for a year at a rate of 2%: it earns €2 million (€100 million × 2%). When the rate was -0.5%, from 2019 to 2022, the same deposit would have cost the bank €500,000 a year, before exemptions.

short: The United Kingdom's central bank, founded in 1694, which sets Bank Rate through its Monetary Policy Committee and oversees UK financial stability.
kid: The Bank of England is a very old helper, older than your great-great-great-grandparents, that looks after Britain's coins and notes and keeps them steady.
detail: The Bank of England, founded in 1694 and based on Threadneedle Street in London (hence its nickname, the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street), is the UK's central bank and one of the oldest in the world. It gained operational independence over interest rates in 1997. Its nine-member Monetary Policy Committee sets Bank Rate, the UK policy rate, to meet the 2% CPI inflation target set by the government, and it also buys and sells bonds. The Bank supervises banks and insurers through the Prudential Regulation Authority and watches system-wide risks through its Financial Policy Committee. A common confusion for Indian readers: the BoE's Bank Rate is its main policy rate, while the RBI's bank rate is a secondary penal rate; the RBI's equivalent of the BoE's Bank Rate is the repo rate.
example: The BoE raised Bank Rate fourteen times in a row between December 2021 and August 2023, from 0.1% to 5.25%, an increase of 515 basis points (5.25 - 0.10 = 5.15 percentage points).

short: Japan's central bank, known for years of near-zero and negative interest rates and huge bond-buying programmes aimed at ending falling prices.
kid: In Japan, prices stayed still or even went down for a very long time. The Bank of Japan tried hard to wake them up, like gently pushing a sleepy friend's swing.
detail: The Bank of Japan, founded in 1882 and based in Tokyo, sets monetary policy for Japan. After years of flat or falling prices, it adopted a 2% inflation target in 2013 and launched massive quantitative and qualitative easing under Governor Haruhiko Kuroda. In 2016 it introduced a negative short-term rate of -0.1% and yield curve control, which capped 10-year government bond yields. In March 2024 it ended negative rates, its first hike in 17 years, and scrapped yield curve control, starting a slow normalisation. Because yen rates were so low for so long, investors borrowed cheaply in yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad, the yen carry trade, so BoJ shifts can trigger sudden global moves, as in August 2024. The BoJ also owns a large share of Japanese government bonds and has bought equity ETFs, unusual for a central bank.
example: In March 2024 the BoJ lifted its short-term policy rate from -0.1% to a range of 0-0.1%, ending eight years of negative rates. A bank that had been charged on ¥100 billion of affected reserves at -0.1% stopped paying ¥100 million a year (¥100 billion × 0.1%).

short: China's central bank: it sets interest rates, decides how much cash banks must set aside and manages the yuan, under the government's direction.
kid: China's big money helper looks after the coins for a huge number of people. It listens closely to the country's leaders when it makes its choices.
detail: The People's Bank of China, founded in 1948 and headquartered in Beijing, is China's central bank. Unlike the Fed or the RBI, it is not independent: it works under the State Council, so policy also serves growth and stability goals set by the government. It uses a wide toolkit: the seven-day reverse repo rate, its main policy rate since 2024, the medium-term lending facility, the reserve requirement ratio (China's version of CRR) and informal window guidance to banks. The one-year and five-year loan prime rates, which price most loans and mortgages, are set monthly by panel banks but follow PBoC signals. It also fixes a daily midpoint for the yuan against the dollar, and onshore trading may move up to 2% either side. Note that a PBoC reverse repo injects cash into banks, the opposite of the RBI's usage.
example: Say the PBoC cuts the reserve requirement ratio by 0.5 percentage point. A bank with ¥1 trillion of deposits subject to the requirement can lend out an extra ¥5 billion (¥1 trillion × 0.5%).

short: An institution in Basel, owned by central banks, that serves as their bank and hosts the committees that write global banking rules.
kid: Imagine all the grown-ups who look after each country's piggy bank meeting in one clubhouse. They keep some of their own coins there and agree on fair rules together.
detail: The Bank for International Settlements was set up in 1930 in Basel, Switzerland, originally to handle German reparation payments after the First World War. Today it is owned by about 60 central banks, including the RBI, which joined in 1996, and serves them as a bank: it takes their deposits, holds part of their reserves and settles transactions between them. It also hosts the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, whose Basel I, II and III accords set global standards for bank capital and liquidity that the RBI applies to Indian banks. Its research and Annual Economic Report are closely read by policymakers. Basel rules are not law in themselves: they bind only when national regulators adopt them. In Indian news, BIS usually means the Bureau of Indian Standards, so check the context.
example: Under the global Basel III minimums, a bank needs common equity tier 1 capital of 4.5% of risk-weighted assets plus a 2.5% conservation buffer. A bank with risk-weighted assets of ₹2,00,000 crore therefore needs at least ₹14,000 crore (7% × ₹2,00,000 crore); the RBI sets stricter levels for Indian banks.

short: How a central bank manages interest rates and the amount of money in the economy to keep inflation low and support steady growth.
kid: When everyone has lots of pocket money, the sweet shop raises its prices. The grown-ups make pocket money a little easier or harder to get, so prices stay steady.
detail: Monetary policy is the set of actions a central bank takes to influence the cost and availability of money and credit. Its main lever is the short-term policy rate, such as the RBI's repo rate or the Fed's federal funds rate, backed by liquidity operations, reserve requirements, asset purchases and communication. Tightening (higher rates, less liquidity) cools spending and inflation; easing does the opposite. Effects travel through the transmission mechanism: money-market rates, bank lending and deposit rates, bond yields, the exchange rate, asset prices and expectations, usually with lags of several quarters. In India the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee runs monetary policy under an inflation target. Do not confuse it with fiscal policy, which is the government's taxing, spending and borrowing; the two interact but are run by different bodies.
example: Say inflation is running at 6% against a 4% target and the central bank raises its policy rate from 6.00% to 6.50%. If banks pass this on, a ₹10 lakh business loan costs ₹5,000 more interest a year (₹10,00,000 × 0.5%), and some borrowing gets postponed, cooling demand.

short: The six-member RBI panel that votes on India's repo rate and policy stance, usually at six meetings a year.
kid: Six people sit around a table and vote on one important choice for the whole country, like friends voting on which game to play. If it is a tie, the leader decides.
detail: India's Monetary Policy Committee was created by a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act and first met in October 2016. It has six members: the RBI Governor (chair), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer nominated by the central board, and three external experts appointed by the government for four-year terms. Each member has one vote, and the Governor has a casting vote in a tie. The law requires at least four meetings a year, though in practice it meets about every two months. It decides the policy repo rate and states a stance; the resolution is published on the day, and minutes, with each member's vote and reasoning, follow about two weeks later. Note that the Bank of England also has an MPC, and in economics textbooks MPC can mean marginal propensity to consume.
example: If four of the six members vote to cut the repo rate by 25 basis points and two vote to hold, the cut passes 4-2. With a 3-3 split, the Governor's casting vote decides, and the minutes later show who voted which way.

short: The Federal Reserve committee that sets the US federal funds rate target and steers the Fed's bond holdings, meeting eight times a year.
kid: Twelve people in America meet a few times a year to decide if borrowing should be easier or harder. The whole world waits to hear what they say, like a class waiting for the bell.
detail: The Federal Open Market Committee is the Fed's policy-setting body. It has twelve voting members: the seven Board governors, the president of the New York Fed, and four of the other eleven regional Fed presidents, who vote on a yearly rotation; all presidents join the discussion. It holds eight scheduled meetings a year and can meet in between if needed. Each meeting ends with a statement on the target range for the federal funds rate, followed by the Chair's press conference. Four times a year it also publishes the Summary of Economic Projections, including the dot plot of members' rate expectations, and minutes appear three weeks after each meeting. FOMC decisions move global markets, including Indian stocks, bonds and the rupee the next morning. The Chair has only one vote, so dissents are recorded and watched closely.
example: Say the FOMC lowers its target range from 3.75-4.00% to 3.50-3.75%. That is a 25 basis-point cut, and overnight lending between US banks is then expected to trade inside the new, lower range.

short: A central bank's scheduled announcement of its interest-rate decision and outlook; in India, the RBI's policy statement released about every two months.
kid: Every few weeks, the grown-up in charge of the country's piggy bank stands up and tells everyone the plan, like a coach explaining the next game.
detail: A monetary policy review is the regular cycle in which a central bank assesses the economy and announces its policy. In India, the RBI Governor announces the MPC's decision on the repo rate and stance, usually at 10 a.m. on the last day of a three-day meeting, along with growth and inflation projections and a separate statement on developmental and regulatory measures. Six reviews a year make it a 'bi-monthly' policy, meaning once every two months, not twice a month. The older name 'credit policy' dates from when the RBI announced policy only once or twice a year. Markets react to more than the headline rate: the vote split, the stance, the forecasts, liquidity measures and the Governor's tone often matter more. Bond yields, bank stocks and the rupee are usually the most sensitive.
example: Say a review keeps the repo rate unchanged but raises the year's inflation projection from 4.0% to 4.5%, with a 4-2 vote to hold. Bond traders may read it as hawkish and sell, pushing the 10-year government bond yield from 6.30% to 6.38%, a rise of 8 basis points.

short: The main short-term interest rate a central bank sets to signal and steer how expensive borrowing is across the economy.
kid: Think of it as the master dial on the town's piggy bank. Turn it up and borrowing gets harder for everyone; turn it down and it gets easier.
detail: The policy rate is the benchmark interest rate a central bank controls directly and uses as its main instrument. Each central bank defines it differently: the RBI's policy repo rate, the Fed's target range for the federal funds rate, the ECB's deposit facility rate and the Bank of England's Bank Rate. The central bank keeps overnight money-market rates close to it through liquidity operations and standing facilities, and changes then pass through to bank lending and deposit rates, bond yields and the currency. Markets watch both the level and the expected path, because asset prices react to surprises, not to fully expected moves. Do not confuse the policy rate with what you pay or earn: home-loan and FD rates are set by banks, usually as a spread over a benchmark. For current levels, check the live rates board rather than any fixed number.
example: Say the policy rate rises from 5.50% to 6.00%. That is a 50 basis-point hike, because 1 basis point is 0.01 percentage point, yet it is a rise of about 9% in the rate itself ((6.00 - 5.50) / 5.50 = 0.091).

short: The rate at which the RBI lends to banks overnight against government bonds as security; India's main policy interest rate.
kid: When a friend's piggy bank is empty for a day, they borrow a few coins from the class helper and leave a toy as a promise. Tomorrow they give back the coins plus one sweet as thanks.
detail: Repo is short for repurchase agreement. A bank sells government securities to the RBI and agrees to buy them back, typically the next day, at a slightly higher price; the difference works out to interest at the repo rate. The repo rate has been India's single policy rate since 2011 and has been set by the MPC since 2016; the RBI tries to keep the overnight call money rate close to it. It sits in the middle of the policy corridor, between the Standing Deposit Facility rate below and the Marginal Standing Facility rate above. Since October 2019 banks have had to link new floating-rate retail and small-business loans to an external benchmark, and most chose the repo rate, so changes now reach many home-loan EMIs at the next reset. Common confusion: the repo rate is not what customers pay; banks add a spread on top.
example: Say a bank borrows ₹1,000 crore overnight from the RBI at a repo rate of 6%. Interest is ₹1,000 crore × 6% × 1/365 = about ₹16.44 lakh, so it repays about ₹1,000.16 crore the next day.
formula: Repo interest = Amount borrowed × Repo rate × Days / 365

short: The rate the RBI pays banks when they park surplus money with it against government bonds; now largely replaced by the Standing Deposit Facility.
kid: When a friend has extra coins they do not need today, they lend them to the class helper and hold a toy as a promise. Tomorrow they get their coins back plus a small sweet.
detail: In a reverse repo the RBI borrows from banks: it sells them government securities and agrees to buy them back later at a slightly higher price, so banks earn the reverse repo rate on surplus funds. For years it was the floor of the policy corridor, set a fixed gap below the repo rate. During Covid it was cut in steps to 3.35% by May 2020, an unusually wide 65 basis points below the 4% repo rate. In April 2022 the RBI introduced the Standing Deposit Facility, which needs no collateral, as the new floor; the fixed-rate reverse repo, left at 3.35% as of 2025, now operates only at the RBI's discretion, and variable rate reverse repo auctions handle larger absorptions. Confusion to avoid: 'reverse' is named from the RBI's side, and China's central bank uses 'reverse repo' for injecting cash, the opposite of Indian usage.
example: Say a bank parks ₹2,000 crore with the RBI overnight at a reverse repo rate of 3.35%. It earns about ₹18.36 lakh (₹2,000 crore × 3.35% / 365); at an SDF rate of, say, 5.75% it would earn about ₹31.51 lakh, which is why banks prefer the SDF.
formula: Reverse repo interest = Amount parked × Reverse repo rate × Days / 365

short: An RBI window where banks park spare money overnight and earn interest; its rate sets the lowest point of India's short-term rate band.
kid: If you have extra coins at the end of the day, you can drop them in the teacher's safe box and get them back tomorrow with a tiny extra treat. You never get less than that treat.
detail: The Standing Deposit Facility, introduced by the RBI in April 2022, lets banks deposit surplus funds with the RBI, usually overnight, at the SDF rate, set 25 basis points below the policy repo rate under the framework as of 2025. Its key feature is that it is uncollateralised: unlike in a reverse repo, the RBI does not have to hand over government securities, so its capacity to absorb liquidity is not limited by its bond holdings. A 2018 amendment to the RBI Act made this possible. Because banks can always earn the SDF rate, none should lend overnight for less, so it acts as the floor of the policy corridor, replacing the fixed-rate reverse repo. Large SDF balances signal surplus liquidity and pull call money rates towards the floor. Confusion to avoid: it is a facility for banks, not a deposit scheme for the public.
example: Say the repo rate is 6.00%, so the SDF rate is 5.75%. A bank parking ₹5,000 crore overnight earns about ₹78.77 lakh (₹5,000 crore × 5.75% / 365).
formula: SDF rate = Policy repo rate - 0.25 percentage point (corridor rule as of 2025)

short: An emergency RBI window where banks borrow overnight at a rate above the repo rate; it sets the upper limit for India's overnight rates.
kid: If a friend runs out of coins and nobody else will share, the teacher will always lend some, but asks for a bigger treat back. So nobody ever has to pay more than that.
detail: The Marginal Standing Facility, introduced in 2011, lets banks borrow overnight from the RBI when other sources dry up. The MSF rate is set 25 basis points above the policy repo rate under the framework as of 2025, which makes it a penalty rate and the ceiling of the policy corridor: no bank should pay more than this for overnight money. Its special feature is that banks may pledge part of the government securities they must hold for SLR, dipping below their SLR requirement up to a limit (2% of NDTL, broadly deposits, under rules as of 2025). Heavy MSF borrowing is a stress signal that liquidity is tight. India's Bank Rate has been aligned with the MSF rate since 2012. Confusion to avoid: the MSF is a standing facility that banks can use on demand, unlike repo auctions, which the RBI chooses when to hold.
example: Say the repo rate is 6.00%, so the MSF rate is 6.25%. A bank short of ₹500 crore that borrows through the MSF overnight pays about ₹8.56 lakh (₹500 crore × 6.25% / 365), about ₹34,000 more than at the repo rate (₹8.22 lakh).
formula: MSF rate = Policy repo rate + 0.25 percentage point (corridor rule as of 2025)

short: In India, an RBI reference rate used mainly to set penalties on banks that miss reserve rules; it equals the RBI's emergency lending rate.
kid: The teacher keeps an old rule card in the drawer. Today it is mostly used to decide how big the fine is when someone forgets to keep their coins in the class box.
detail: Under Section 49 of the RBI Act, the Bank Rate is the standard rate at which the RBI is prepared to buy or rediscount bills of exchange and other commercial paper. It was once a key policy signal, but since the repo rate became the operating policy rate, the Bank Rate has been a secondary rate. In February 2012 the RBI aligned it with the Marginal Standing Facility rate, so it moves automatically whenever the MSF rate changes, which is 25 basis points above repo under the framework as of 2025. Its main use today is as the base for penal interest when banks fall short of CRR or SLR requirements, and as a reference in some laws and contracts. Big confusion: in the UK, 'Bank Rate' is the Bank of England's main policy rate, closer in role to the RBI's repo rate.
example: Say the repo rate is 6.00%, so the MSF rate and Bank Rate are both 6.25%. If a bank's CRR balance falls ₹100 crore short for a day and the penalty is Bank Rate plus 3 percentage points, it pays about ₹2.53 lakh (₹100 crore × 9.25% / 365).

short: The share of deposits that Indian banks must keep as cash with the RBI, earning no interest; cutting it frees money for lending.
kid: Every time friends give you coins to look after, you must put a few in the teacher's locked box. You cannot use those coins, but they keep everyone safe.
detail: The cash reserve ratio is the percentage of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL, broadly its deposits and certain other liabilities) that it must hold as a cash balance with the RBI under Section 42 of the RBI Act. The RBI pays no interest on these balances, so CRR is effectively a cost for banks. Banks maintain it on a fortnightly average basis, with a minimum each day. Changing CRR alters durable liquidity at once: a cut releases funds banks can lend or invest, a hike locks them up. For instance, the RBI cut CRR by 50 basis points to 4% in December 2024, releasing about ₹1.16 lakh crore, and in June 2025 announced a phased cut to 3%. Do not confuse CRR with SLR: CRR is cash parked with the RBI, while SLR assets, mostly government bonds, stay with the bank and earn interest.
example: Say a bank has NDTL of ₹1,00,000 crore and CRR is 4%. It must keep ₹4,000 crore with the RBI; if CRR is cut to 3.5%, the requirement falls to ₹3,500 crore, freeing ₹500 crore to lend or invest.
formula: Required CRR balance = CRR % × Net demand and time liabilities (NDTL)

short: The share of deposits Indian banks must hold in safe, easy-to-sell assets such as cash, gold and government bonds, kept by the bank itself.
kid: For every bag of coins friends give you to look after, you must keep a few in a very safe jar you can open quickly. That way you can always give friends their coins back.
detail: The statutory liquidity ratio is the minimum percentage of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that it must keep in liquid assets: cash, gold and unencumbered approved securities, mainly central and state government bonds and treasury bills. It is set under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, which caps it at 40% under the law as of 2025. Unlike CRR, SLR assets stay on the bank's own books and earn interest. SLR does two things: it keeps a cushion of safe assets for depositors, and it creates steady demand for government debt, which critics call financial repression. The required level has been cut over the decades, but most banks hold more than the minimum because many of these bonds also count towards the Basel III liquidity coverage ratio. Do not confuse it with the US supplementary leverage ratio, also abbreviated SLR.
example: Say a bank has NDTL of ₹50,000 crore and SLR is 18%. It must hold at least ₹9,000 crore in approved assets; if it actually holds ₹12,000 crore of government bonds, the extra ₹3,000 crore is excess SLR it can pledge to borrow.
formula: Required SLR holding = SLR % × Net demand and time liabilities (NDTL)

short: The RBI's toolkit for adding or removing short-term cash in the banking system through short loans to banks and deposit windows.
kid: Some days a few friends have extra coins and some have too few. The teacher keeps a box where spare coins can rest and a jar that short friends can borrow from, so everyone gets through the day.
detail: The Liquidity Adjustment Facility, introduced in stages from 2000, is the set of operations through which the RBI manages short-term liquidity in the banking system so that overnight rates stay close to the policy repo rate. Its operating target is the weighted average call rate (WACR), the average rate on overnight interbank borrowing. When banks are short of funds, the RBI injects money through fixed-rate repo, variable rate repo (VRR) auctions and, at a penalty, the Marginal Standing Facility. When there is a surplus, it absorbs money through the Standing Deposit Facility and variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions. The net LAF position, absorptions minus injections, is the daily liquidity gauge that bond and money-market traders watch. Confusion to avoid: LAF handles short-term, day-to-day liquidity; lasting shifts are managed with OMOs, CRR changes and forex swaps.
example: Say on one day banks borrow ₹30,000 crore through repo and MSF and park ₹1,10,000 crore in the SDF and VRRR. The net LAF position is an absorption of ₹80,000 crore (₹1,10,000 - ₹30,000 crore), so the system is in surplus.
formula: Net LAF position = Funds absorbed (SDF + reverse repo + VRRR) - Funds injected (repo + VRR + MSF)

short: The band between a central bank's deposit rate (floor) and its emergency lending rate (ceiling), within which overnight market rates are kept.
kid: Imagine two ropes on a playground, one low and one high. Everyone has to play between the ropes, and the teacher stands right in the middle.
detail: An interest rate corridor is the range set by two standing facilities: a deposit facility where banks can always park money (the floor) and a lending facility where they can always borrow (the ceiling). Since no bank should lend for less than the central bank pays, or borrow for more than it charges, overnight market rates stay inside. In India the floor is the SDF rate and the ceiling the MSF rate, each 25 basis points from the repo rate under the framework as of 2025, giving a 50 basis-point corridor; the RBI aims to keep the weighted average call rate near the repo rate in the middle. Where rates sit inside the band reveals liquidity: near the floor means surplus, near the ceiling means shortage. The ECB's three key rates also form a corridor, though, like the Fed, it now steers rates through a floor system with ample reserves.
example: Say the repo rate is 6.00%. The SDF floor is then 5.75% and the MSF ceiling 6.25%, a 50 basis-point corridor; if the call rate trades at 5.80%, close to the floor, the system has surplus liquidity.
formula: Corridor width = MSF rate - SDF rate

short: An RBI auction that lends money to banks for a set number of days, with banks bidding the rate they will pay.
kid: When lots of friends need to borrow coins at once, the teacher asks how big a thank-you treat each will give back. Those offering the biggest treats get the coins first.
detail: A variable rate repo is an auction-based repo in which the RBI announces how much it will lend and for how long, from overnight to 14 days or more, and banks bid the amount they want and the rate they will pay, at or above the repo rate. The RBI fills the highest bids first until the notified amount is used up; the lowest accepted rate is the cut-off. VRR auctions are the RBI's main tool for injecting short-term liquidity when the system is in deficit, for example around advance-tax and GST payment dates, when money flows out of banks into the government's account. Unlike the fixed-rate repo, the price is set by bidding, so cut-off rates well above repo signal tight liquidity, while weak demand shows banks need less money. Confusion to avoid: VRR adds money; VRRR, with the extra R, takes it out.
example: Say the RBI offers ₹50,000 crore in a 7-day VRR auction and banks bid for ₹80,000 crore. The bid-to-cover ratio is 1.6 (₹80,000 / ₹50,000 crore), and only bids at or above the cut-off, say 6.02% with repo at 6.00%, are filled.
formula: Bid-to-cover ratio = Total bids received / Amount notified

short: An RBI auction that takes surplus money from banks for a set number of days, with banks offering the interest rate they will accept.
kid: When friends have more coins than they need, the teacher asks who wants to leave some in the safe box for a few days. Those happy with the smallest thank-you treat get picked first.
detail: A variable rate reverse repo is the absorption counterpart of the VRR. The RBI announces how much surplus it wants to drain and for how long, and banks offer funds at rates they choose, usually between the SDF rate and the repo rate. The RBI accepts the lowest-rate offers until the notified amount is filled. Because it can lock money away for several days rather than overnight, the RBI uses VRRRs when surplus liquidity is large and is dragging overnight rates towards the floor of the corridor, which weakens the pass-through of the policy rate. They gained prominence as the RBI unwound the Covid-era surplus from 2021, shifting absorption away from the fixed-rate reverse repo. Bigger VRRR amounts often reflect heavy government spending or strong capital inflows. Confusion to avoid: VRRR removes money; VRR adds it.
example: Say the RBI holds a ₹1,00,000 crore 3-day VRRR and banks offer ₹1,40,000 crore. It accepts the lowest-rate offers up to ₹1,00,000 crore, so ₹40,000 crore of offers is turned away and those banks park the money in the SDF instead.

short: A central bank's buying or selling of government bonds in the open market to add or remove money from banks for the long term.
kid: When the teacher buys toys from the children with coins, the children have more coins to spend. When the teacher sells toys back, the coins return to the teacher.
detail: Open market operations are outright purchases or sales of government securities by the central bank. When the RBI buys bonds (an OMO purchase), it pays by crediting banks' accounts, adding durable liquidity; when it sells (an OMO sale), money flows back to the RBI, draining liquidity. Unlike repos, which reverse within days, OMOs change liquidity until the bonds mature. They also move bond prices: purchases support prices and push yields down. The RBI conducts OMOs mainly through auctions, and in 2021 it ran a pre-announced G-sec Acquisition Programme (G-SAP) of ₹1 lakh crore in April-June and ₹1.2 lakh crore in July-September. OMOs often offset liquidity drains from forex intervention or cash demand. Confusion to avoid: OMO purchases are a liquidity tool and are not automatically quantitative easing, which means much larger, policy-driven buying, usually after rates hit zero.
example: Say the RBI buys ₹20,000 crore of government bonds from banks in an OMO auction. Banks' reserves with the RBI rise by ₹20,000 crore and their bond holdings fall by the same amount, so system liquidity improves by ₹20,000 crore.

short: A central bank buying long-term government bonds while selling short-term ones at the same time, to lower long-term rates without adding money.
kid: The teacher swaps the children's long skipping ropes for short ones, one for one. Nobody ends up with more ropes, but long ropes become rarer and more special.
detail: Operation Twist is a simultaneous purchase of long-maturity government bonds and sale of a similar amount of short-maturity ones. Because the central bank's buying supports long-bond prices, long-term yields tend to fall, while short-term yields may rise slightly: the yield curve twists and flattens. Since the purchases and sales offset each other, overall liquidity barely changes, which makes it a way to lower long-term borrowing costs, such as mortgage and corporate bond rates, without expanding the money supply. The name comes from a 1961 Fed and US Treasury programme, and the Fed repeated it as its Maturity Extension Program in 2011-12. The RBI ran a series of such 'special OMOs' from December 2019. Confusion to avoid: it is not QE, because the size of the central bank's balance sheet barely changes.
example: Say the RBI buys ₹10,000 crore of 10-year bonds and sells ₹10,000 crore of bonds maturing within a year in one operation. Net liquidity is unchanged (₹10,000 - ₹10,000 crore = 0), but extra demand for 10-year paper might pull its yield from 6.80% to 6.60%, a fall of 20 basis points, while one-year yields edge up.

short: Central-bank loans to banks for long periods, from months to years, at low rates, to cut funding costs and support lending in stressful times.
kid: Usually the teacher lends coins only until tomorrow. In hard times the teacher lends them for a whole year or more, so friends can plan their lemonade stands without worrying.
detail: Long-term repo or refinancing operations give banks central-bank funding for far longer than the usual overnight or one-week window. In India, the RBI introduced long-term repo operations in February 2020, lending for one and three years at the policy repo rate so banks could lock in cheap funds and cut loan rates. During Covid it added targeted LTROs (TLTROs), where the money had to go into corporate bonds, commercial paper and debentures, including those of NBFCs and microfinance lenders. In Europe the ECB's longer-term refinancing operations played a similar role: its two three-year LTROs in December 2011 and February 2012 lent banks about €1 trillion during the euro debt crisis, and later TLTROs rewarded banks that lent more to businesses. Confusion to avoid: these are loans that must be repaid, not outright bond purchases like QE.
example: Say a bank borrows ₹2,000 crore through a three-year LTRO at a fixed 5%. It pays ₹100 crore of interest a year (₹2,000 crore × 5%), or ₹300 crore over three years, and keeps that cost even if market rates rise to 6%, which would cost ₹120 crore a year.

short: How much spare cash banks collectively hold beyond what they need, measured by how much they borrow from or park with the central bank.
kid: At the end of each day, the teacher checks whether the whole class has spare coins or is running short. Spare coins make borrowing easy; running short makes it hard.
detail: Banking system liquidity is the net amount of reserves in the banking system relative to banks' needs. In India it is usually read from the net LAF position: when banks park more with the RBI (through the SDF and VRRR) than they borrow (through repo, VRR and MSF), the system is in surplus; the reverse is a deficit. Core or durable liquidity also counts the government's cash balance with the RBI, giving a longer-lasting view. Liquidity moves with forces beyond the policy rate: cash demand around festivals and elections, tax payments that move money into the government's account, government spending, RBI forex intervention (selling dollars drains rupees), OMOs and CRR changes. A surplus pushes overnight rates towards the corridor floor and can ease conditions without any rate cut; a deficit does the opposite. Confusion to avoid: this is about cash in the banking system, not how easily a stock trades.
example: Say advance-tax payments move ₹1,50,000 crore from company bank accounts to the government's account at the RBI in mid-June. A system that had a ₹1,00,000 crore surplus swings to a ₹50,000 crore deficit (₹1,00,000 - ₹1,50,000 crore), and call rates may rise above the repo rate.
formula: Net liquidity (India) = Funds absorbed by RBI under LAF - Funds injected by RBI under LAF

short: A central bank's signal of which way it is leaning on future interest rates: ready to cut (accommodative), neutral, or ready to raise.
kid: Before a game, the coach tells the team whether they will play gently, normally or extra hard next time. That way nobody is surprised.
detail: The policy stance tells markets the likely direction of the next moves, separate from today's rate decision. The RBI's MPC states its stance explicitly in each resolution. 'Accommodative' means it is ready to cut rates or keep liquidity ample to support growth; 'neutral' means it could move either way depending on data; phrases such as 'calibrated tightening' (2018) and 'withdrawal of accommodation' (used from 2022 to 2024) signal a bias towards higher rates or tighter liquidity. The Fed and ECB convey stance through statement wording rather than a single label. A stance change can move markets more than a rate change because it resets expectations: a shift from accommodative to neutral can lift bond yields with no change in the rate. Confusion to avoid: stance describes intent, not the current level, so a rate cut can come with a neutral stance, as in June 2025.
example: Say the MPC holds the repo rate but changes its stance from neutral to accommodative. Traders price in future cuts, and the 10-year bond yield might fall from 6.40% to 6.30%, 10 basis points, on the day, even though the repo rate is unchanged.

short: When a central bank makes money costlier or scarcer, by raising rates, draining cash or shrinking its bond holdings, usually to cool inflation.
kid: When the shop's prices keep jumping up, the grown-ups make borrowing pocket money a bit harder. People buy a little less, and prices calm down.
detail: Monetary tightening, also called contractionary or restrictive policy, is any central-bank action that raises borrowing costs or reduces the money available. The main tools are rate hikes, draining liquidity (for example through VRRR auctions, OMO sales or a CRR increase) and quantitative tightening, which shrinks the bond holdings built up under QE. The aim is to slow demand and anchor inflation expectations. Effects arrive with a lag: loan rates rise, borrowing and spending slow, bond yields rise and long-bond prices fall, and equity valuations often compress, especially for growth stocks and rate-sensitive sectors such as real estate, autos and NBFCs, while the currency tends to strengthen. A tightening cycle is a series of hikes. Confusion to avoid: policy is truly restrictive only when the rate is above the neutral rate; a hike from a very low level can still leave policy loose.
example: Between May 2022 and February 2023 the RBI raised the repo rate six times, from 4.00% to 6.50%, a total of 250 basis points (6.50 - 4.00 = 2.50 percentage points).

short: When a central bank makes money cheaper or more plentiful, by cutting rates, adding liquidity or buying bonds, usually to support growth.
kid: When people stop buying lemonade and the stand goes quiet, the grown-ups make borrowing pocket money a little easier. People spend more, and the stand gets busy again.
detail: Monetary easing, also called expansionary or accommodative policy, is any central-bank action that lowers borrowing costs or increases the money available. Tools include rate cuts, liquidity injections (VRR auctions, OMO purchases, CRR cuts, long-term repos) and, when rates are near zero, quantitative easing and forward guidance. The aim is to support spending, investment and jobs when growth is weak and inflation is under control. Typical market effects: bond yields fall and bond prices rise, equity valuations tend to rise with rate-sensitive sectors such as real estate, autos and NBFCs often leading, floating-rate loan EMIs drop, and the currency may weaken. An easing cycle is a series of cuts. Confusion to avoid: a cut can upset markets if it signals that the central bank sees a sharp slowdown, and cuts help borrowers but lower returns for fixed-deposit savers.
example: Between February and June 2025 the RBI cut the repo rate three times, by 25, 25 and 50 basis points, taking it from 6.50% to 5.50%, a total of 100 basis points.

short: When a central bank keeps its policy rate unchanged after a run of hikes or cuts, while keeping the option to move again.
kid: After pushing the swing higher and higher, you stop pushing for a moment to see how it goes. You might push again later, or let it slow down.
detail: A rate pause is a decision to hold the policy rate after a series of changes, usually to let earlier moves work through the economy, since monetary policy acts with lags of several quarters. The market's key question is what kind of pause it is. A 'hawkish pause' keeps the door open to more hikes; a pause with softer language may mark the peak of the cycle. The RBI surprised markets in April 2023 by pausing at 6.50% after 250 basis points of hikes, with Governor Shaktikanta Das calling it a pause, not a pivot. The Fed's June 2023 hold was widely described as a 'skip' because it hiked again in July. Confusion to avoid: a pause means 'no change for now', while a pivot is a change in direction, such as moving from hikes to cuts; markets often misread pauses as signs of imminent cuts.
example: After its last hike in February 2023, the RBI kept the repo rate at 6.50% for eleven consecutive policy meetings, from April 2023 to December 2024, before cutting it by 25 basis points to 6.25% in February 2025.

short: A clear change in a central bank's direction, such as switching from raising interest rates to holding or cutting them.
kid: You are walking one way down the path, then you turn around and walk the other way. That turn is a pivot.
detail: In market language, a pivot is a turning point in central-bank policy, most often a move from tightening to easing (a 'dovish pivot'); a 'hawkish pivot' runs the other way. Markets obsess over pivots because asset prices move on expected changes: bonds and growth stocks can rally months before the first cut if investors believe a pivot is coming. A classic case is the Fed in early 2019, which switched from planned hikes to patience and then cut later that year. Through 2022-23 investors repeatedly bet on a 'Fed pivot' that arrived only in September 2024, when the Fed began cutting with a 50 basis-point move. A pivot usually shows up first in words, through the stance, forward guidance or projections, before any rate move. Confusion to avoid: a single pause is not a pivot, and in startup news 'pivot' means changing the business model.
example: Say a central bank has raised its rate from 2% to 5% over 18 months and then signals that its next move is likely a cut. Two-year bond yields might drop from 4.8% to 4.3%, a fall of 50 basis points, before any cut actually happens.

short: A central-bank rate cut announced between scheduled policy meetings, usually in response to a sudden crisis or market shock.
kid: Normally the teacher changes the class rules only on Mondays. But if something scary happens on a Wednesday, the teacher may change them right away to help everyone.
detail: An emergency, or inter-meeting, rate cut is made outside the central bank's published meeting calendar. Because central banks prize predictability, such moves are rare and kept for severe shocks: financial crises, pandemics or sudden market seizures. Examples include the coordinated 50 basis-point cut by six major central banks, including the Fed, ECB and Bank of England, on 8 October 2008; the Fed's 50 basis-point cut on 3 March 2020 and 100 basis-point cut on Sunday 15 March 2020; and the RBI's off-cycle cuts of 75 basis points on 27 March 2020 and 40 basis points on 22 May 2020. Markets read them two ways: relief that policymakers are acting, and alarm that things are bad enough to need it, so stocks sometimes fall on the news. Confusion to avoid: emergency moves are not always cuts; some emerging-market central banks make emergency hikes to defend their currency.
example: On 15 March 2020 the Fed cut its target range by 100 basis points, from 1.00-1.25% to 0-0.25%, less than two weeks after a 50 basis-point emergency cut from 1.50-1.75%; together that is 150 basis points outside the normal schedule.

short: A central bank's public statements about where interest rates are likely to go, used to shape expectations and longer-term borrowing costs today.
kid: If the teacher tells the class that snack time will stay the same all month, everyone can plan their day. Just saying it calms everyone down.
detail: Forward guidance is communication about the likely future path of policy. Because long-term rates reflect expected short-term rates, a credible signal that rates will stay low can lower bond yields and loan rates today, which is why it became a key tool once rates hit zero after 2008. Forms vary: open-ended ('for an extended period'), calendar-based (rates low 'at least through mid-2013', said by the Fed in 2011) and state-contingent (no hikes while unemployment stayed above 6.5%, the Fed's 2012 threshold). The Fed's dot plot and the RBI's stance and inflation projections are softer forms. Economists separate Delphic guidance, a forecast, from Odyssean guidance, a commitment. Confusion to avoid: guidance is conditional, not a promise; when the data change, so does the path, as markets learned in 2021-22 when inflation forced rapid hikes.
example: Say a central bank signals it will keep its policy rate at 1% for two more years. Investors expect overnight rates near 1% for that period, so a two-year bond yield might settle around 1.2% instead of the 2% it would trade at if hikes were expected, saving borrowers 0.8 percentage point.

short: A central bank's approach of deciding policy meeting by meeting based on the latest economic data, instead of following a pre-set path.
kid: Before deciding whether to wear a coat, you look out of the window each morning instead of choosing for the whole week. That is how a careful helper decides.
detail: A data-dependent central bank sets each decision according to incoming information on inflation, jobs, growth and financial conditions, rather than committing to a path in advance. The Fed has used the phrase heavily since 2022, and the RBI's MPC regularly stresses that it will stay watchful and decide meeting by meeting. The benefit is flexibility in uncertain times, especially after forward guidance proved costly when inflation surged in 2021. The cost is less predictability: markets react more sharply to each data release, such as US payrolls or India's CPI print, because any one of them can change the next decision, and bond yields and currencies can swing on a single number. Confusion to avoid: data dependence does not mean reacting to one month's figure; central banks look at trends and forecasts, and some data, such as core inflation, carry more weight.
example: Say markets price a 60% chance of a Fed cut at the next meeting. A US CPI print of 0.5% month-on-month against a forecast of 0.2% could drop that to a 20% chance within minutes, because a data-dependent Fed is now less likely to cut.

short: Said of a central bank that has reacted too slowly to inflation or a slowdown, so it must later make bigger, more painful moves.
kid: If you leave for the bus stop too late, you have to run very fast to catch the bus. Leaving early means you can just walk.
detail: A central bank is behind the curve when its policy lags what economic conditions require, most often when inflation rises faster than rates. Because policy acts with long lags, waiting too long lets inflation become embedded in wages and expectations, forcing steeper hikes later and raising the risk of recession. The best-known recent case is the Fed in 2021, which called inflation 'transitory' and held rates near zero, then had to raise them by 525 basis points in about 16 months from March 2022. The opposite, ahead of the curve, describes pre-emptive moves, such as hiking before inflation takes hold or cutting before a downturn deepens. The idea applies to easing too: a bank that cuts too late into a recession is also behind the curve. Confusion to avoid: the 'curve' here is not the yield curve; it simply means the path of the economy.
example: Say inflation jumps from 2% to 7% while the policy rate stays at 0.25%. The real policy rate is then about -6.75% (0.25% - 7%), deeply negative, and a central bank in that position is widely described as behind the curve.

short: A central bank creating new money to buy large amounts of bonds, pushing down long-term interest rates when short-term rates are already near zero.
kid: When the teacher has already made snacks as cheap as they can go, they start buying the children's stickers with brand-new coins, so everyone has more coins to spend and play with.
detail: Quantitative easing is large-scale buying of government bonds, and sometimes other assets such as mortgage or corporate bonds, paid for with newly created central-bank reserves. It is used when the policy rate is already near zero and further cuts are not possible. QE works by lowering long-term yields, pushing investors into riskier assets, lifting asset prices and signalling that rates will stay low. The Fed ran three rounds after 2008 and bought heavily again in 2020; its balance sheet grew from under $1 trillion in 2007 to nearly $9 trillion in 2022. The BoJ, ECB and BoE ran large programmes too, and the RBI's 2021 G-SAP was sometimes called India's QE. Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse. Confusion to avoid: QE is not literally printing banknotes or handing money to people; it creates bank reserves in exchange for bonds.
example: Say the Fed buys $100 billion of Treasury bonds from banks and dealers. It pays by creating $100 billion of new reserves, so its balance sheet grows by $100 billion on both sides: bonds as assets, reserves as liabilities.
